translations.text: I have heard that Holofernes then eagerly sent out invitations to wine and prepared a feast in splendour, with every kind of wonder.
Then they went to sit at the feast, proud men to the wine-drinking, all his companions in woe, bold warriors in mail-coats.

There deep bowls were carried again and again along the benches, and cups and pitchers too, full, to those sitting in the hall. They took the drink, doomed men, brave shield-warriors, though the powerful one did not expect it, the fearsome lord of nobles.

Then Holofernes, gold-friend of men, grew merry with the pouring of wine. He laughed and shouted, roared and made a din, so that the children of men could hear from far away how the stern-minded one stormed and yelled, arrogant and flushed with mead. Again and again he urged those sitting on the benches to enjoy themselves well.

So all day long the wicked one, the stout-hearted giver of treasure, drenched his retainers with wine, until they lay in a stupor. He made his whole troop of veterans so drunk that they lay as if struck down by death, drained of every good.
So the lord of men ordered the hall-sitters to be served until dark night drew near to the children of men.
Then, filled with malice, he ordered the blessed maiden to be fetched quickly to his bed, laden with bracelets, adorned with rings.
But the Judge of glory, the Guardian of majesty, would not allow it. Instead he kept him from that deed: the Lord, ruler of hosts.
Then he had met an unpleasant end on earth, such as he had worked for before, the harsh-minded prince of men, while he lived in this world under the roof of the clouds.
The warriors went out of the chamber in great haste, men sated with wine, who had led the oath-breaker, the hateful tyrant, to bed for the last time.
My heart is now fiercely inflamed and my mind is sad, sorely troubled with sorrows.
I have never had greater need of your mercy. Avenge now, mighty Lord, glorious-minded giver of glory, what so angers my mind and burns hot in my breast."

He need not hope at all, wrapped in darkness, that he may get out of that hall of serpents. Instead he shall stay there for ever and ever, without end, from then on, in that dark home, without the joys of hope.
The warriors sat; the men kept watch and guard in the fortress, as Judith had earlier commanded the sad-hearted people when she set out on her journey, the shrewd-minded maiden, the courageous lady.
and spoke these words to the victorious people: "I can tell you something to be thankful for: you need not mourn in your hearts any longer.

The Creator, the glory of kings, is gracious to you. It has been made known far and wide throughout the world that splendid glorious success is coming to you, and glory is granted to you for the injuries you have long suffered."
Then the people living in the city were glad, once they heard how the holy one spoke over the high wall. The army rejoiced.

The people hurried toward the fortress gate, men and women together, in crowds and masses, in throngs and troops. They pressed forward and ran by the thousands to meet the Lord's maiden, old and young.
The heart of every man in that mead-city was gladdened when they saw that Judith had come back to her homeland, and they quickly and humbly let her in.
Then the noble one spoke to all the people: "Here, victorious heroes, leaders of the people, you can see clearly and gaze on the head of the most hateful heathen warrior,
This was harshly paid back to all of them, the Assyrians, in the play of ash-spears, after the Hebrews had marched under their battle-banners to the army camps.

With their hands the warriors drew brightly adorned swords from their sheaths, swords with proven edges. Grimly they struck the Assyrian warriors, who had hostile intentions. They spared none of that army, neither lowly nor powerful, none of the living men they could overcome.
So the young retainers pursued the foreigners all through that morning, until those who were hostile, the army's chief guards, realized that the Hebrew men were showing them fierce sword-strokes.

They went to report this in words to the most senior chief officers. They roused the standard-bearing warriors and fearfully announced the sudden news to them: to the mead-weary men, a morning terror, a dreadful play of swords.
Then at once, I have heard, the warriors doomed to die shook off sleep, and with weary hearts they crowded in throngs toward the pavilion of the evil one, Holofernes.
They meant to announce the battle to their lord immediately, before the terror, the might of the Hebrews, came down upon him.
They all supposed that the lord of warriors and the radiant maiden were together in the beautiful tent: Judith the noble and the lustful one, terrible and fierce.

A mighty people fought them from behind, until the greatest part of the army lay felled in battle on the field of victory, hewn down by swords, a pleasure to the wolves and also a comfort to the slaughter-greedy birds.
Then boldly, with gleaming swords, the brave-hearted warriors cut a path for the army through the throng of their enemies. They hewed the linden-wood shields and cut through the shield-wall.

The defenders of the homeland had gloriously overcome their enemies on that battlefield and put their old foes to sleep with swords. Those who, of all living peoples, had been most hateful to them in life lay at rest along their track.
…everything that the men of the nation, bold under their banners, had won gloriously in battle through the wise counsel of Judith, the courageous maiden.
As a reward, the spear-brave warriors brought back to her from that expedition Holofernes's sword and bloody helmet, and also his broad coat of mail adorned with red gold,
